entries.title: [Editorial] RFK Jr and MAHA: dangerous, emboldened, and escalating
entries.description: The week beginning Aug 4, 2025 was the most dangerous and tragic week of Robert F Kennedy Jr's tenure yet: a fatal CDC shooting by a gunman distrustful of COVID-19 vaccines, the cancellation of US$500 million in mRNA research funding, and his malicious call to retract a peer-reviewed Annals of Internal Medicine paper on vaccine safety. RFK Jr has built an increasingly powerful movement in Make America Healthy Again (MAHA). Either through incompetence or disinformation, the actions of this movement pose the greatest threat to the health of Americans and millions of people globally.

entries.title: [Correspondence] INTERLACE: not a new standard for cervical cancer chemoradiation
entries.description: In the prospective EMBRACE-I study, chemoradiotherapy with image-guided adaptive brachytherapy (IGABT) reached unmatched outcomes and has since become the standard treatment for locally advanced cervical cancer.1,2 In 2023, after decades of high-level evidence against additional systemic therapies, the randomised INTERLACE trial was presented as a congress abstract, showing improved survival by adding induction chemotherapy to standard chemoradiotherapy. Induction chemotherapy was suggested as a new universal standard, prompting its growing adoption.

entries.title: [Health Policy] Surgical health policy 2025–35: strengthening essential services for tomorrow's needs
entries.description: Progress towards The Lancet Commission on Global Surgery's 2030 targets has been too slow and too patchy, particularly in low-income and middle-income countries. The unmet need for surgery has continued to grow, reaching at least 160 million operations per year. Ensuring high-quality surgical care remains a crucial global challenge, with 3·5 million adults dying after surgery each year. The COVID-19 pandemic exposed the fragility of surgical services long undermined by chronic underfunding, workforce shortages, and under-resourced infrastructure.

entries.title: [Perspectives] Shakira Choonara: upholding health and rights for young people
entries.description: “Almost half of the world's population are women, and the latest stats show us that less than 50% of women and girls have power over their health-care decisions”, says Shakira Choonara, a passionate public health practitioner and activist working in the multilateral agency space. Her current focus area is sexual health and reproductive rights (SRHR) and bodily autonomy. Choonara wants to see governments boost investment for SRHR, given the current backlash from certain groups. “SRHR is under attack, and so ramping up and scaling up investments is important”, she comments.

entries.title: [Articles] Safety and efficacy of steroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists in patients with kidney failure requiring dialysis: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
entries.description: Our findings suggest that steroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists have little to no effect on cardiovascular mortality in patients requiring dialysis. There is insufficient information on the effects of steroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists in subgroups of patients requiring dialysis and no information on non-steroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists. Future trials would need to consider the likelihood of only smaller effects or effects limited to patients or events with pathophysiology that is more clearly driven by aldosterone in their design.

entries.title: [Perspectives] Creative challenges to misinformation
entries.description: Two anatomy books, open at the sections describing female genital anatomy, are currently on display at the State Library of Victoria, Melbourne, VIC, Australia. Both have been defaced. In Quain and Wilson's 1842 Series of Anatomical Plates, a direct source for the first edition of Gray's Anatomy, the page devoted to “Female Organs of Generation” is patched up with tape after repeat vandalism by generations of readers who must have felt there was something inherently obscene about documenting female biology.

entries.title: [Correspondence] Humility and curiosity in human–AI systems for health care
entries.description: A woman aged 62 years presents with shortness of breath. Her chest x-ray is interpreted as normal by an artificial intelligence (AI) triage system. The overworked resident, reassured by the system's apparent confidence, discharges her. Days later, she returns in cardiac arrest with missed signs of heart failure. This scenario reflects a systemic breakdown where over-reliance on the model eclipsed clinical reasoning. The AI delivered a confident verdict precisely because it was programmed to do so, as it does not have the mechanisms to communicate uncertainty.

Between 2000 and 2024, measles incidence in the USA only exceeded one case per 1 million population in three of these years, with a peak of 3·8 cases per 1 million population in 2019 (1272 cases) and 1319 cases in 2025 by July 22 (>50 cases in Texas and New Mexico).

entries.title: NASA’s Bennu Samples Reveal Complex Origins, Dramatic Transformation
entries.description: Asteroid Bennu, sampled by NASA’s OSIRIS-REx mission in 2020, is a mixture of dust that formed in our solar system, organic matter from interstellar space, and pre-solar system stardust. Its unique and varied contents were dramatically transformed over time by interactions with water and exposure to the harsh space environment. These insights come from a trio of newly published papers based on the analysis of Bennu samples by scientists at NASA and other institutions.

entries.title: Why tiny bee brains could hold the key to smarter AI
entries.description: Researchers discovered that bees use flight movements to sharpen brain signals, enabling them to recognize patterns with remarkable accuracy. A digital model of their brain shows that this movement-based perception could revolutionize AI and robotics by emphasizing efficiency over massive computing power.

entries.title: Jupiter’s core isn’t what we thought
entries.description: For years, scientists thought Jupiter’s strange interior was the result of a massive collision in its youth. But new research suggests that the planet’s diffuse, “fuzzy” core wasn’t born from a cataclysm at all. Instead, the giant appears to have developed this structure gradually as it pulled in both heavy and light elements while forming.

entries.title: Scientists discover forgotten particle that could unlock quantum computers
entries.description: Scientists may have uncovered the missing piece of quantum computing by reviving a particle once dismissed as useless. This particle, called the neglecton, could give fragile quantum systems the full power they need by working alongside Ising anyons. What was once considered mathematical waste may now hold the key to building universal quantum computers, turning discarded theory into a pathway toward the future of technology.

entries.title: Tiny quantum dots unlock the future of unbreakable encryption
entries.description: By using quantum dots and smart encryption protocols, researchers overcame a 40-year barrier in quantum communication, showing that secure networks don’t need perfect hardware to outperform today’s best systems.

entries.title: These asteroids share a strange fingerprint from billions of years ago
entries.description: Scientists studying asteroids found that two seemingly unrelated types share a strange dusty coating of troilite. By using polarization of light instead of traditional spectra, they uncovered evidence that these space rocks may have originated from the same ancient parent bodies, offering a new glimpse into the chaotic past of the early solar system.

entries.title: What came before the Big Bang? Supercomputers may hold the answer
entries.description: Scientists are rethinking the universe’s deepest mysteries using numerical relativity, complex computer simulations of Einstein’s equations in extreme conditions. This method could help explore what happened before the Big Bang, test theories of cosmic inflation, investigate multiverse collisions, and even model cyclic universes that endlessly bounce through creation and destruction.
